score_meanings.promise_vocabulary: 0 drifts into claims/profiles/central trust-ledger framing, 5 stays promise-first and pCID-specific
score_meanings.simplicity_durability: 0 overbuilt or fragile, 5 minimal, durable, and small-device-friendly under the 100-year goal

promise_theory_rules: A promise is a scoped declaration of intent.
No agent can make a promise on behalf of another agent.
Trust is a local assessment of whether a promise will be kept.
Promises to receive or use are not equivalent to obligations, impositions, or promises to give.
promise_theory_references: Mark Burgess, In Search of Certainty
Mark Burgess, Promise Theory: Principles and Applications

assessment.rationale: Strong on auditable, local evidence and boundary separation, but only indirectly addresses relationship-scoped adoption. It helps peers state scoped implementation boundaries, yet it does not explicitly model Bob promising one profile to Alice and another to Carol. Promise Theory fit is decent but vocabulary still leans on claim cards and audit-ledger artifacts rather than plain promise statements.
strengths: Exact audit-anchor citation improves later local audit.
Clear live/audit/storage/device separation prevents cross-layer overclaiming.
Break-witness handling is honest under ambiguous physical-effect replay.
Evolution is supported through provisional IDs and rotation references.
weaknesses: Scenario pressure is only partially met because relationship context is not explicit.
Promise vocabulary is mixed with claim-card and status terminology.
Artifact set is somewhat heavy for small, durable deployments.
risks: Claim cards may become de facto normative compliance artifacts instead of scoped promises.
Operators may treat audit records as global trust ledgers.
Per-relationship adoption differences may remain ambiguous and look like equivocation.
open_questions: How would Bob express different adoption promises to Alice and Carol without turning claim cards into peer-global assertions?
Are capability/auth notes explicitly relationship-scoped, or only embodiment-scoped?
What local record shape distinguishes legitimate per-peer variation from broken promises?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.

autonomous_agents.note: Peers publish their own cards and keep local append-only records; no central controller is required.

scoped_intent.note: Plane-scoped cards and exact audit anchors express bounded intent clearly.

no_promises_for_others.note: The simulation mainly has each peer speak for its own embodiment and records.

no_guaranteed_outcomes.note: The design distinguishes receipts, failures, retention observations, and break-witnesses rather than guaranteeing success.

local_trust_assessment.note: Trust is supported by locally checkable anchors and records, but 'audit ledger' framing can be misread as shared authority.

accept_use_not_obligation.note: Mostly compatible, but the scenario's relationship-scoped adoption semantics are not explicit in the artifact design.

violations: Uses claim-card/status/conformance-style wording instead of consistently stating agent promises.
Audit-ledger framing risks drifting toward globally authoritative trust evidence.
Relationship-scoped adoption is underspecified, so peer-pair-specific promises are not first-class.
